lede: For a month this archive knew him as two index entries: «military records for 1840 and 1841», and a death in Devon in 1885. He was the eldest son of Joseph D'Arcy and the grandson of Robert, and he governed two colonies on opposite sides of the Atlantic. Everything below came out of free, official sources that had been open the whole time — and was found by searching, instead of his surname, the one word in his name that nothing else in print shares.

name.head: The name is the evidence
name.body: ABBAS KOOLY is Abbas Qoli, for Prince Abbas Mirza of Persia, whom his father served five years. This archive knew that before it knew anything about the son, because it is in Joseph's own obituary. So the identification of a «George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy» in the Gazette does not rest on the name being unusual, though it is the most unusual in these pages — it rests on the name's origin being documented here already. A boy baptised at Westminster on 31 August 1818 is eighteen when the War Office gazettes him an Ensign in the spring of 1837.

career: A Gazette memorandum that exists only to correct the War Office: «The Christian names of Ensign D'Arcy, of the 94th Regiment of Foot, are George Abbas Kooli.» He was eighteen.
«Ensign and Adjutant George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy to have the rank of Lieutenant.»
«Adj. Geo. Abbas Kooli [D']Arcy» in both monthly volumes. These are the «military records for 1840 and 1841» this archive carried for a month as a bare phrase and had never identified.
The Army List, 1840, January–June and July–December
«Lieutenant George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy to be Captain, vice Davenport.» Printed independently in a trade paper the following month.
London Gazette, issue 20664, p.4260; The Military Magazine, December 1846
The Southern Mahratta and Sawant-Warree campaign, under Brigadier Outram

He was also aide-de-camp and assistant private secretary to five successive governors of Bombay, and to Sir Willoughby Cotton commanding the Bombay army. His brother Robert West married at Bombay in January 1846.
«Captain George Abbas Kooli d'Arcy, from the 94th Foot, to be Major, by purchase.» Fifteen years in one regiment, then a West India corps.
«Major George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy to be Lieutenant-Colonel, by purchase, vice Murray, who retires.» Gazetted in London on the 7th and in Edinburgh on the 11th.
He left the army, and was a colonial governor within the year.
Governor and Commander-in-Chief of the Gambia
«Colonel George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy to be Governor and Commander-in-Chief in and over Her Majesty's Settlements in the River Gambia» — gazetted in the same sentence as the new Governor of Hong Kong.
He commanded the Gambia militia artillery in the field. He had already organised an expedition against the robber-king of Baddiboo, for which he received the thanks of the Secretary of State.
At forty-eight hours' notice he embarked against a Marabout invasion and carried an entrenched position. Two officers were killed at his side.

The European merchants gave him an address and a sword of honour worth £120, «for devoted bravery at the storming of Tubabecolong, and to mark their appreciation of his administration of the government».
«W. F. C. Robinson, 1866. Colonel D'Arcy, 1870. T. F. Callaghan, 1876» — the Colonial Office's own list of Falkland governors. Two colonies and an ocean between them.
He is absent from the Colonial Office Lists for 1883 and 1889, both read entire, which is what retirement looks like.
The Colonial Office List for 1883 and 1889
As «George Abbas-Kooli D'Arcy». The death rests on the GRO index alone; no obituary has been found.

vc.head: A Victoria Cross was won following him through a stockade
vc.body: At Tubabecolong in 1866 the Colonial Office List records that two officers were killed at his side — Lieutenants Kelly and Jenkins of the 4th West India Regiment — with four soldiers, two volunteers, four of the native contingent and sixty-one of all ranks badly wounded. And then one sentence: «Private Samuel Hodge, who followed Colonel D'Arcy through the stockade, received the Victoria Cross.» Hodge was among the first black soldiers to receive it. He is not this archive's to tell, and he is here because the record puts him at this man's shoulder.
vc.note: The 1877 entry describes the invading force in the racial language of its period. That phrase is not reproduced on this page, because nothing in this family's history turns on it.

open: Whether he ever married is not known. The Colonial Office notice names his regiments, his campaigns, his book and his sword, and says nothing of a wife; four George D'Arcy marriages in the English index between 1837 and 1890 carry none of his forenames, in quarters FreeBMD marks above 99% transcribed. He spent most of his adult life outside English registration, so a marriage at Bathurst or in the West Indies would not be in that index at all.
method: He was found by searching the Internet Archive's full text for «Abbas Kooli» — not for «D'Arcy». The surname is mangled by every OCR that touches it, into «D'Aroy» and «Darcy» and worse, and the forename drowns in Georges. The middle name survives everything, because nothing else in print looks like it. That is the whole trick, and it is worth more than this page.
